posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Off the bat, I have to "upvote" RNG drops as being bad design.  Yet another thing dragged into singleplayer RPG's that only existed in MMO's, and only exists THERE for a specific reason.
I have never been happy with having to grind kills on an enemy to "get a good drop" or even "get a God Roll drop".  I personally think that the only people who enjoy such mechanics are probably people who have "addictive personalities".  IE:  Gambling Addiction is probably in their future.
The only time I like "grind" in a game is when I choose to do it.  Not when the dev has designed some system that forces me to do it.  I will grind levels when I want to skip the next set of combat stuff.  That's fine.  Grinding enemies for drops is awful, especially if I'm only doing it as a completionist/collector.
I'm in a singleplayer RPG guys, my collection only matters to ME here.  So, there's no reason to make obtaining that collection DIFFICULT.
Even in MMO's, it has to be done WELL to be worth it.  If what I grind for in an MMO isn't cared about by the wider community and nobody stops me to ask me "how did you get that?", then there should be no grind associated with obtaining it.  The journey has to mean something to OTHER PLAYERS for the piece of gear TO BE MEANINGFUL in an ONLINE SPACE.
Even "Raid Gear" In MMO's is often pretty "worthless" for that.  It often has problems of not looking cool, is useless outside of raid content (raid gear, the only gear that makes raids easier, and doesn't do anything else for any other content!  So, it's only coveted by people who play raids!  Everyone else will ignore it and not care you have it!), and has unreasonably steep requirements to obtain it (like timegating!).
Just give me the drops in the normal course of the game.  Or let me buy them.
On to other games/systems that are "the worst".
Chaned Echoes
The combat mechanic of "walk a tight rope" is bad.  It forces you to use weak attacks so you don't eat lots of damage, which also forces you to play every single combat with the same exact method to "keep within the green zone".  It's boring.  It's unnecessarily complex.  And, it suffers from a design flaw I hate in any video game:  Negative Design.
There's probably a better phrase for it, but it's basically anytime you do something the dev doesn't want you to do, you get punished.  Rather than, you know, incentivizing you to do stuff by rewarding you, it just punishes you for doing stuff it doesn't like.
"Oop, you used your overpowered skill too much, time to punish you by making you take 2x or 3x more damage per enemy hit!".
The "skillpoint" system in this game is also a serious problem since it only awards you skillpoints at specific points of the story (according to the game itself, and when it explained that, I quit playing) rather than at level up.  It's obvious it only does this so you can't immediately break the combat "tightrope" system.  Because, if I can wipe your enemies with 1 hit, I don't have to bother with your clunky and boring system.
Which is, honestly, how I bypass "stagger" systems in games, too.  Powerlevel, overlevel, then ignore the stagger mechanics (why anyone on the planet ever thought these were fun, I have no idea, but God bless the players who think having their own time wasted is heaven!  You're the reason mobile games are so popular, and so are loot boxes, and anything EA does!).
Borderlands 3
The story.  Dear God, this story is stupid.  Here's the story:
Badguys, "Hey, we're gonna use this key to open all the vaults!"
Heroes, "Hey, we stole the key from you, but it's not charged, so it can't open any vaults.  Let's charge it up!"
Badguys, "Hey, thanks for doing all the work for us!"
That's the whole game.
I'm not even getting into the walking atrocity that is Ava, either.  She can die in a fire and any dev on that team who thought she was a good idea, should never write for video games again.
I also had problems with the loot system.  Namely that almost all of the loot in the game is worthless, plus the usual RNG problems of any other system.
Chrono Cross
Honestly... this would have probably been a good game if it had never been tied to Chrono Trigger.  I went into this game expecting masterful storytelling like Chrono Trigger and fun/quick combat with double/triple techs... and the game delivered exactly 0% of a Chrono Trigger experience.
It really probably would've done a lot better without the expectations of "This is a Chrono Trigger sequal" saddled to it.  But, since it was created and marketed that way... well... I went in comparing it to Chrono Trigger at every opportunity.  And, it fell short, everywhere I looked.  In the end, I just went back and played Chrono Trigger again rather than finish it.
---
Let's get into "individual systems".
Stagger
I just generally don't like any system that is not "make enemies dead".  Anything that extends the length of combat time into "I'm wasting time here", is not something I generally enjoy.
If filling the stagger bar doesn't kill the enemies faster than if I were killing enemies in a regular RPG WITHOUT the stagger bar... then just remove it.  I'm not interested in spending my finite resource known as "time" in a game that has "not fun" mechanics.
Timed...
I'm also just generally not interested in RPG's that have "time limits".  I don't mind Timers in games.  Unless you pair them with specific things.  I have the same issue with Timers in RPG's that Ross Scott does with Timers in Puzzle games.
If you give me a Timer in a game system that generally requires strategies and decision making... I do not want to be rushed.  At all.
I can react fast to situations, or I can make decisions.  I cannot do both.  Stop asking of me that I do both.  My brain does not do so well when you're asking me to THINK FAST and ACT FAST at the same time.
Also, I just usually don't like engaging with games that have "time limits".  What if I want to play forever?  What if I want to do everything?  Well, now I need a guide for that, which sucks ALL THE FUN out of the game.
Just one of the reasons I've never even tried the "Persona" series of games.  I'm not interested in replaying a 70+ hour game because I ran out of time to do things or didn't play "the most optimal way" on my first run.  Just... no thank you.
Pointless stats/skills
Easiest example I can think of:  Anything that is "reduce radiation" in Fallout 3, 4, and 76.  I have thousands of Radaway, why do I need to "reduce radiation damage"?  I don't.  Waste of perks.
There are a lot of RPG's with fairly useless stats/skills that just don't do anything useful or meaningful.  Skyrim basically has anything in the Restoration series of spells (they don't heal enough to be useful, so potions are far better... or... even better than that... stockpiling your level ups so you can burn one when you're about to die for a free "refill everything" button).
I'm also not really fan of those stats/skills that are useless being deliberate "newbie traps".
---
Alright, that's my short list.  Meh.

For me, the problem isn't RNG, it's the
very common
misuses of RNG. There's plenty of ways of changing it that would
barely
change how a given mechanic works that would make things far better. For some examples;
Rare drops. There's nothing inherently wrong with getting something rare for defeating an enemy. The problem is when you
only
get it this way and thus
must
rely on randomness to let you have something. I brought more major fixes to this problem earlier, but the far simpler solution is a building chance so that you can kill X enemies and get it guaranteed. Maybe it's a 1% drop chance that increases to 2% if you don't get it, then 3%, and resets when you do eventually get the item
I can't believe I'm suggesting a gacha mechanic
. Worst case scenario you fight 100 of that enemy, but at least you know you will eventually get it, making it a marginally better form of grinding. But, my favorite way I personally use rare drops is to only pick items you can buy later. You can get a platinum axe three dungeons early and that's
awesome

A state that chooses your targets for you (say, Confusion or Daze). then

Accuracy. A 9.75% chance you do nothing with your turn is just... boring. And having all your possible options deal with that 9.75% means you just have to deal with a weighted coin every single turn. On the flipside, having a 'default' 100% accuracy with options to gamble gives a risk-reward system; Do you pick the safe option that will work, or the strong option that can end enemies faster that might not? Back when it was anticipated that you would play a game many times and then keep coming back to it when there weren't any other new games you wanted to play.
In Wizardry 8 there are a few such instances where there is a very small chance of getting a specific item from a specific encounter. But the key is that you don't actually need those items to complete the game. And anyone who wants to sit and grind reloads to try to get it certainly can if that's what they want to do. I actually like randomness in games. I don't think that every player needs to have the same experience and I think randomness can give games more replay value.

Save Points - I hate Save Points. I want to save when I want to save because I never know when I need to stop playing. Let me play the way I want or need to play.
Ridiculous gold rewards and pricing - I mean what kind of economy does the game have when a basic sword costs 350, 700, 1,500 gold pieces? Who even makes that kind of money and how do they carry it around? You open a chest and find 10,000 gold! Hmmm...good luck carrying that around.
Non-Choices - If the choices don't really mean anything, don't offer them to me.
Making me play a specific way to be successful - I get that there are optimal party or character builds/combinations or items, skills, etc. or tactics that would/should be more useful against certain enemies. Party wipes as a mechanic to set up the story or whatever - I don't like the mechanic in general, but if you absolutely must do it, just make it a cut scene and don't give me any control over the combat and make it seem like I could win.

Freedom said:
For those who don't like RNG, what would you want instead?
Click to expand...
Which I will ALSO answer, because I think it's an important essence of this thread.
What's important is to keep in mind what RNG systems are trying to accomplish, what experiences they want to create and prevent. The important step is that there are very many scenarios where straight RNG will FAIL to create these experiences
because
it is purely random, and thus we tweak things with subsystems.
There is an incredibly diverse array of methods to control RNG for a better player experience, and most of them can be applied to any type of game. But the code debt may accumulate to such a degree that only a few will end up actually being used, if the dev was even aware of all of them.
Spark/Pity Systems - Almost exclusively used in gacha games, this is a clumsy, brute force, and ultimately unsatisfying solution for everyone. It is used only due to a legal and financial obligation to guarantee a minimum level of value to the spender, and a minimally sufficient tool to control the player's gambling addiction. And yet it's still less painful that trying to steal a flute off a Hill Giant.
Availability Creep - Most commonly in the form of making the items available in shops later, this also includes stronger enemies simply having higher chances of dropping the item. As the game progresses, you transition the item from being something rarely available to common, maintaining its initial novelty without completely missing content if the rare item never dropped. This is especially important for sidegrade and specialized gear, or small amounts of permanent power increases.
Conditional Drops - Instead of using random chance, you have to follow a particular step to unlock the drop. Etrian Odyssey is fairly famous for this, but it can be as simple as burning the tree monster to get burnt wood drops. This trades random chance for compatibility, as certain party builds will generally get certain drops more often based on their quirks. If it is based on status ailments, you are also playing with larger, more standardized infliction rates. Working with 20-30% chances is far more enjoyable than 3% drops, and you will be able to confirm the drop BEFORE the actual kill. Conditional Drops are also a means of creating optional difficulty or alternate experiences when facing one particular enemy. Don't forget that you can make these mutually exclusive, essentially making route splits for stuff you get.
Drop Rate Creep - Somewhat of a fusion of Conditional Drop and Availability Creep. In its simplest form, it is being able to equip loot-boosting gear. Generally, that sucks ass because it homogenizes player builds. But what TWEWY is famous for is creating a system of artificial de-leveling to boost your drop rates, universally making loot easier to get as you get stronger, and as long as you are willing to challenge yourself. Let me be clear: this has flaws. It still doesn't do a good job of creating asymmetrical loot experiences, and you can end up with a LOT of unwanted clutter.
Taste of Power - While most games only show you high level stuff early to take away later, there is the option of creating singular, story-gated instances of random rewards 1 or 2 tiers beyond the current point of the story. This will color how you adapt your regular gear to make use of these, and you will be able to familiarize yourself with the new mechanics going forward when it becomes a regular drop. You DO, however, need to MAKE these pools of early freebie gear that has to be curated. Random monster bits are much harder to be certain they'll be useful.
Taking 20 - The thing with 3% Steal and 2% Drop is to communicate an intention to the game that if you can prove you can roll forever, you should be able to get it without actually rolling forever. So kill chains like FF12 are very effective for this, as well as doing something like spending 10 consecutive turns stealing without taking damage or some such.
Thematic RNG - Sometimes it's enough to control the range of possible loot. You don't want to give the player the exact same meta sword, but they DO want a sword, so there should be an option to get a decent sword in 3 rolls. Path of Exile pays particular attention to this, and it'll be interesting to see how much further Path of Exile 2 takes it.
Narrative Weight - Sometimes the important thing isn't the RNG at all. The item is proof of the unique experience, rather than the creator of it. If you only get this item if you went into this hidden path to find the forest lake and experienced an event not everyone goes out of their way to get......that's fine!

There are some things I absolutely dislike, such as characters whose strength is totally different from how the story depicts them. At the same time, I personally dislike long dialogues that make the game longer for no reason while you have to keep pressing the same button over and over again.
However, that is my subjective opinion and, as such, its value when defining bad mechanics is nearly zero. Trying to go a bit deeper into this topic to give an objective standpoint on this matter, the "bad mechanic" per se is something that does not exist. As it has already been mentioned above, it is its implementation that might be bad.
Spoiler:
Why enemies scaling in FF8 is a bad implementation
One example of bad implementation is FF8 enemies scaling. Is enemies scaling bad at all? Not really, it helps to keep up the challenge, but it becomes bad when it punishes whoever played the game. From a mathematical standpoint, as you keep playing, your strength also increases, when this happens, equipment gets proportionally weaker the stronger you are. Normally, this is not an issue because you got more powerful overall. When you apply this to a game with scaling enemies mechanics, however, especially when enemies scaling has the same curve as the player's scaling, your gear gets proportionally weaker in an absolute sense, since your power gain compared to enemies is zero.
Does this make scaling enemies something bad? No, but it gives a hint about HOW it should be done: players strength gain from playing the game should be proportionally higher than the strength loss from equipment being less relevant, so enemies scaling shall be tuned around that.
This applies also to other mechanics, as those related to RNG (random loots, random skills, etc.), but that much has already been covered in detail in other previous posts, so I will not spend more words on that.

Oh goodie, a thread where I can vent frustration about certain mechanics that drive me crazy in RPGs and will most likely result in me refunding the game:
Random encounters.  This one's pretty obvious and most people hate it, but it's especially bad when the rate is high.  Anyone ever play Breath of Fire 2?  It's like here you are, exploring an area when all of a sudden, you get interrupted.  You get rid of it, take a few more steps, then another interruption.  I've had times when I forgot which way I was going because of so many back-to-back encounters.
Level-scaling enemies.  I could be wrong, but I'm pretty sure the original concept behind leveling up in RPGs was to give the player a sense of progression as well as to reward the extra time with an easier time against otherwise-challenging content.  Having enemies scale with player levels destroys literally all of this.
Tightly-limited inventory.  Having to stop story or exploration just to sort out which random widgets I need vs which ones I don't...sucks.  I get that in some cases you need some sort of limit, in particular when working with instanced items, but if my inventory is full and I'm only a few dungeons in?  No thanks.
QTEs.  These are another form of interruption that I find unpleasant.  I don't mind action games, but when I play RPGs, I'm generally in a more relaxed, casual frame of mind.  Having to snap out of that just to press a button at the right time to dodge an attack or open a chest is...unpleasant.  I actively avoid RPGs that I know use these.
Missable content.  The completionist in me just doesn't want to feel obligated to play with a guide open the entire time to avoid missing [item], [party member], etc.  Especially if the steps to get them are obscure or if there's some unexpected event sequence that occurs to cut me off from it.
Omnipresence of certain gimmicky fight mechanics.  Things like guard break gauges that need to be depleted before the enemy can be meaningfully damaged are fine for a boss or two, but having to play that weird minigame on every single enemy fight or even most of the gets old after awhile.
Whew, and there it is!

posts.author: pawsplay
posts.body:
Knights of the  Old Republic
is beloved to many, but to me, it's a litany of design sins, such that I had trouble finishing it and have never bothered to replay it fully.
Intrusive mini-games:
Collecting cards was a tiresome chore, and the racing game was not a good racing game. There were a couple of Encyclopedia Brown type mysteries which were perplexing, not very logical, and offered scant rewards for the effort. At least the rings puzzles gave me nostalgia for middle school.
Law of Conservation of XP:
The game is mostly linear, and each area has a limited number of encounters, apart from a handful of random encounters you can farm by traveling between systems. Missing stuff can mean becoming critically underpowered in the next act, and woe to you if you make sub-optimal class choices. If you miss content, you might need to grind dozens of encounters with raiders or ghouls to make just one more level to gain a key trait.
Thematic Failure:
Some of the best combinations in the game were not I was looking for in a Jedi game. In particular, stub-locking enemies and then cutting them up felt weird, and even the most pure-hearted Jedi found it purely advantageous toward the end of the game to do a brief stint as a paid hitman and acquire venomous Sith weapons, which were ideal for the final boss fight.
Trap Choices:
Pick Your Difficulty Level is a legitimate thing, and people like to play games in different ways. But choosing a Scoundrel was just, not just challenging, but meh, as they have neither the Soldier's attack bonus nor the Scout's durability and cybernetic implants. Stealth is rarely relevant, almost never optimal, and equipment and strategy matter far more than skill ranks. Similarly, the Jedi Guardian is a straightforward choice, and the Consular is okay. But the Sentinel has the same attack bonus at the Consular, nearly as good powers, and much better skills. There is no reason to play anything than either a Soldier or Scout who turns into a Guardian or Sentinel. A Scoundrel/Counselor just doesn't have enough oomph in any department to feel fun.
FOMO:
Hidden or bonus content is one thing, but when a linear game pushes you past early stages, causing you to miss out on XP, vital equipment, or the resolution of relationship dynamics, that's just disappointing. I don't mind replaying to try to get everything, but I don't like being expected to play again to repair my experience by doing everything right the second time.

This way, players would at least know which attribute allocation suits their playstyle.
